articles/clients.html.title: Connecting clients | Uniform Chat Server
articles/clients.html.summary: Connecting clients Log in with the full user ID and the homeserver address http://localhost:8008. In Element, edit the homeserver on the sign-in page. In the Uniform Chat terminal client, give the address with --Matrix:Homeserver: ./Uniform.Chat --Matrix:UserId=@alice:localhost --Matrix:Homeserver=http://localhost:8008 Without an address, clients find the server from the user ID: they look for https://<server name>/.well-known/matrix/client. That needs a real server name, HTTPS and Server:PublicBaseUrl.

articles/dashboard.html.title: Run with the dashboard | Uniform Chat Server
articles/dashboard.html.summary: Run with the dashboard In the unpacked folder: ./uniform-chat-server When started from a terminal, the server opens its dashboard and serves at http://localhost:8008: ┌Matrix server localhost───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ File Server │ │ Listening: http://localhost:8008 │ │ Uptime: 0:12:31 │ │ Requests: 1520 answered, 3 in progress, 2 failed │ │ Accounts: 4 users, 3 rooms │ │ │ │ Data: /home/alice/.local/share/uniform-chat-server │ │ Log: /home/alice/.local/share/uniform-chat-server/logs/2026-10-26… │ │ │ │ F9 or Alt+F for the menu; Server → Users to create accounts. Ctrl+Q stops it. │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Listening shows the addresses clients connect to. Requests counts client requests: answered, being answered now (syncing clients wait here for news), and failed with a server error. Accounts counts users and rooms, every few seconds. Data is the folder with the database and signing key; see Files. Log is this session's log file. The dashboard refreshes every second. The server keeps serving while menus and windows are open. Key Action F9 or Alt+F Open the File menu File → Settings… View and change the server's settings File → Logs… Read this session's log and earlier ones Server → Users… Create users, reset passwords, give admin rights, deactivate accounts Server → Rooms… See rooms and list them in the public room directory Server → Reports… Review what users reported Help → About The server's version, also in the window's title Ctrl+Q or File → Quit Stop the server Settings window File → Settings lists every option with its current value, where the value comes from, and a description of the selected option. Edit (or Enter) changes the selected option; options with fixed values offer a list. Apply uses a change at once, until the server stops. Options marked ↻, such as the server name and the data folder, take effect only after a restart. Save writes the changes to ~/.config/uniform-chat-server/settings.json, which is read at every start. Reset undoes one step at a time: first an edit that is not applied, then an applied change that is not saved. Pressed again, it removes the option from the settings file on save, so the default applies again. Edited options are marked *, applied but unsaved ones +. Values given on the command line override the settings file. Registration tokens are secret: they are never shown in the window. To open registration for a while, for example: select Server:Registration, choose Open and Apply. New users can register at once. Set it back to Disabled and Apply when they are done. Nothing is saved unless you choose Save. Users window Server → Users lists every account with its display name, logged-in devices, joined rooms, and whether it is an admin, suspended, locked or deactivated. New asks for the user name, such as alice for @alice:localhost, the password twice, and whether the user is a server admin. Registration does not need to be open for this. Password sets a new password for the selected user and logs out all their devices, for example when they forgot it. Admin gives or takes server admin rights. Admins may delete any room alias and change any room's directory listing, and manage the server from a client; see Remote administration. Suspend lets the user read and leave rooms, but not send, join, invite or upload; pressed again, it ends the suspension. Lock makes the server refuse the user's devices until it is pressed again; the devices stay signed in. Deactivate logs out every device of the user and stops them logging in; pressed again, it reactivates the account. Their rooms and messages stay. Rooms window Server → Rooms lists every room with its name, alias, joined members, and whether it is public (listed in the directory) or encrypted. Publish lists the selected room in the public room directory, or removes it. Listing a room does not change who may join; that follows the room's own join rule. Messages of encrypted rooms are encrypted on the members' devices, so the server cannot show or read them. Reports window Users can report a message, a room or another user from their client. Server → Reports lists the open reports, newest first, with who reported, what about and why; the dashboard shows how many are open. The details below the list show the whole reason, and the reported message's text when the server has it. Messages of encrypted rooms cannot be read by the server. Resolve marks the selected report as dealt with, so it leaves the list; pressed on a resolved report, it opens it again. Show resolved shows or hides the resolved reports. Delete removes a report for good, after confirmation. Managing a running server The dashboard also opens on a server that already runs, e.g. as a service, without stopping it: sudo uniform-chat-server manage. It shows the same windows, with the settings applied and saved by the running server itself; Ctrl+Q closes only the manager. See Run without the dashboard and Remote administration. Logs window File → Logs shows the log of this session, and lets you open earlier sessions. Each start writes its own file in logs under the data folder. The newest 20 are kept. Changes made in the Users and Rooms windows are logged, such as Admin created user @alice:localhost, so the log also shows what was done; passwords never appear in it.

articles/files.html.title: Files | Uniform Chat Server
articles/files.html.summary: Files Everything the server keeps is in the data folder, ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-server by default (under $XDG_DATA_HOME when set): File Contents server.db The SQLite database: accounts, devices, rooms and messages. The server updates it to its current layout at start. server.db-wal, server.db-shm The database's write-ahead log and its index, while the server runs; at a clean stop the log is written into server.db. Copy them with the database. media/ Uploaded files, and the thumbnails made from them in media/thumbnails/. signing.key The server's private signing key, which signs every event it creates. It is created when first needed and readable only by your user. logs/ One log file per start of the server, named by the time it started, e.g. server-20261110-104027.log; the newest 20 are kept. With Storage:LogDirectory they are elsewhere: the apt package's service writes them to /var/log/uniform-chat-server. To back up the server, stop it and copy the whole folder. Keep signing.key with the database and keep it private: it is the server's identity.

articles/install.html.title: Installing | Uniform Chat Server
articles/install.html.summary: Installing The server is a Matrix homeserver: it keeps accounts, rooms and messages, and clients such as the Uniform Chat apps or Element connect to it. One program runs it either with a dashboard in the terminal, or without one as a background service. Note The server is in early development. Accounts, rooms, messages, room state and sync work, as do profiles, presence, typing, read receipts, unread counts, push rules and push notifications through push gateways, room tags, previews of linked pages (when turned on), room aliases, the public room directory, user search, files and images with thumbnails, and end-to-end encryption with cross-signing, emoji verification and key backup. Federation with other servers is being built and is off by default: with Federation:Enabled, users can look up profiles on other servers, join their rooms and talk there, and browse their public room directories, and other servers' users can join rooms here. Requirements Linux or Windows; for the dashboard, a terminal that supports UTF-8 and colors Apt install On Debian and Ubuntu, x64 and arm64, install from the apt repository of Uniform Chat, which is kept in its releases on GitHub. Add the repository once, with the key its packages are signed with: sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://github.com/tagcode/Uniform.Chat/releases/latest/download/uniform-chat-archive-keyring.gpg | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/uniform-chat.gpg > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/uniform-chat.gpg] https://github.com/tagcode/Uniform.Chat/releases/ latest/download/" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/uniform-chat.list sudo apt update Then install the server: sudo apt install uniform-chat-server The package sets the server up as a system service, uniform-chat-server, run by the system user uniform-chat, which it creates: What Where Program /opt/uniform-chat/server, also as the command uniform-chat-server Settings /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json Database, signing key, files and logs /var/lib/uniform-chat-server The service is off until you write the settings, see the example setup below, and enable it: sudo systemctl enable --now uniform-chat-server Run without the dashboard tells more about the service. sudo apt upgrade updates the server with the rest of the system and restarts a running service; back up /var/lib/uniform-chat-server first, see Updating. From the release archives Download uniform-chat-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz (or linux-arm64, or win-x64.zip and win-arm64.zip for Windows) from the releases and unpack it anywhere. It needs nothing else installed. The program is uniform-chat-server, or uniform-chat-server.exe on Windows. The docs folder in it has this guide; open docs/index.html in a browser. To run it as a service, see Run without the dashboard. From source Install the .NET 10 SDK; then use dotnet run --project src/Uniform.Chat.Server -- from the repository root in place of the program in the examples below. Example setup A typical server on the internet runs behind a reverse proxy, such as nginx, which holds the HTTPS certificate; the server itself listens on plain HTTP on the same machine only. The example below is for example.org, with federation, sign-up by registration token, and voice calls through a TURN server; change the names, and leave out what you do not use. Write the settings to ~/.config/uniform-chat-server/settings.json of the user that runs the server, or, as a system service, to /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json. Make the file readable only by that user, as it holds secrets. { "Host": { "Ui": "None" }, "Urls": "http://127.0.0.1:8008", "Server": { "ServerName": "example.org", "PublicBaseUrl": "https://example.org", "TrustedProxies": "127.0.0.1", "Registration": "Token", "RegistrationTokens": "a-long-random-token" }, "Federation": { "Enabled": true, "WellKnownServer": "example.org:443" }, "Calls": { "TurnUris": "turn:turn.example.org:3478?transport=udp,turn:turn.example.org:3478?transport=tcp", "TurnSharedSecret": "the TURN server's static-auth-secret" } } Part Why Urls Plain HTTP on this machine only; nginx in front serves HTTPS. Another port than 8008 if something, such as Synapse, uses it. ServerName, PublicBaseUrl The name in user IDs, and the address clients reach; the server announces it in /.well-known/matrix/client. Choose the name before creating accounts. TrustedProxies nginx's address, so that rate limits and logs see each client's own address. Registration, RegistrationTokens Anyone with a token can sign up; share the token with the people you invite. Open lets anyone sign up, Disabled no one. Federation Talk with other Matrix servers. WellKnownServer is announced in /.well-known/matrix/server, so other servers reach this one on port 443 through nginx, and port 8448 need not be open. Calls TURN servers for 1:1 calls, e.g. coturn with use-auth-secret and the same static-auth-secret; the server hands clients time-limited credentials. Leave the section out without a TURN server, or use the built-in one, see Calls through firewalls. Settings lists every option. The nginx site, e.g. /etc/nginx/sites-available/example.org, enabled with a link in sites-enabled, passes Matrix's paths to the server, with a certificate from certbot: # HTTP: certbot's challenges, everything else to HTTPS server { listen 80; listen [::]:80; server_name example.org; location /.well-known/acme-challenge/ { root /var/www/html; } location / { return 301 https://$host$request_uri; } } # HTTPS: clients and other servers server { # HTTP/2 as a listen flag, which nginx before 1.25.1 needs, e.g. Ubuntu's; newer ones prefer "http2 on;" listen 443 ssl http2; listen [::]:443 ssl http2; server_name example.org; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.org/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.org/privkey.pem; # Files people upload; at least Media:MaxUploadSize client_max_body_size 100M; location ~ ^/(_matrix|\.well-known/matrix)/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8008; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host; # Sync waits for new messages, and joining rooms on other servers can be slow proxy_read_timeout 600s; proxy_send_timeout 600s; proxy_buffering off; } } To get the certificate, enable first only the HTTP part, and run: sudo certbot certonly --webroot -w /var/www/html -d example.org sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx For video calls in Element X through the homeserver's LiveKit service, the location line must also pass /livekit/jwt; see Video calls in Element X. Then enable the HTTPS part, reload nginx again, and start the server. Check from another computer that https://example.org/.well-known/matrix/server answers {"m.server":"example.org:443"}; the federation tester then shows whether other servers can reach yours. Leave out the [::] lines when the name has no IPv6 address.

articles/livekit.html.title: Video calls in Element X | Uniform Chat Server
articles/livekit.html.summary: Video calls in Element X Element X, Element Call and other MatrixRTC apps don't call each other directly. They all join a room on a LiveKit server, a media server that forwards everyone's audio and video. Before joining, an app asks the homeserver's authorization service for a LiveKit token, proving who it is with a Matrix OpenID token. The homeserver has that authorization service built in. You run the LiveKit server next to it. Uniform Chat's apps call this way too when the homeserver has LiveKit, so that Element X users can answer. Without it, they call each other directly; see Calls through firewalls. LiveKit server Install LiveKit from livekit.io. It is a single program. Write its configuration, livekit.yaml, with an API key and a secret of at least 32 characters: port: 7880 rtc: tcp_port: 7881 port_range_start: 50000 port_range_end: 60000 use_external_ip: true keys: homeserver: a-long-random-secret-of-at-least-32-characters room: auto_create: false auto_create: false makes sure only your users can start calls. The authorization service creates each call's room for them. Run it with livekit-server --config livekit.yaml. If lk-jwt-service also uses this LiveKit, note that it reads only one key from a key file. Give it a file of its own with just its key, rather than LiveKit's keys list. LiveKit must be reachable from the internet on these ports. Behind a home router, forward them to its computer: Port Protocol Use 443 TCP The apps' WebSocket, through a reverse proxy with a certificate, to LiveKit's 7880 7881 TCP Media over TCP, for networks that block UDP 50000–60000 UDP Media The apps connect to wss://, so put a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of port 7880, at a name such as livekit.example.org. With Caddy, for example: livekit.example.org { reverse_proxy localhost:7880 } Homeserver Turn on the authorization service and point it at LiveKit. Put the secret in the settings file or an environment variable, not on the command line: { "LiveKit": { "Enabled": true, "Url": "wss://livekit.example.org", "ApiKey": "homeserver", "ApiSecret": "a-long-random-secret-of-at-least-32-characters" } } Restart the homeserver after editing its settings file, as it reads the file only on starting. The dashboard's Apply changes the settings of the running server at once, with no restart. The service is then at /livekit/jwt of the homeserver's Server:PublicBaseUrl, and the homeserver announces it to the apps. Only users joined to the call's room get in. Your users can start calls and send audio and video. Users of other homeservers who are in the room can join calls that are already going, but only to watch and listen, unless you add their servers to LiveKit:FullAccessHomeservers. See Settings for every LiveKit setting. A reverse proxy in front of the homeserver must pass /livekit/jwt to it as well. With the nginx site of Installing, add it to the location line: location ~ ^/(_matrix|livekit/jwt|\.well-known/matrix)/ { To check the service, open https://example.org/livekit/jwt/healthz, with your server's address. It answers with an empty page and status 200 when the service is on, and 404 when it is off. Using another service If you already run lk-jwt-service or a separate uniform-livekit-server, leave LiveKit:Enabled off. Set Calls:LiveKitServiceUrl to that service's address, such as https://example.org/livekit/jwt, and the homeserver announces it instead.

articles/remote-admin.html.title: Remote administration | Uniform Chat Server
articles/remote-admin.html.summary: Remote administration Besides the dashboard on the server's own machine, admins can manage the server from a client, over the same address the clients use. Only accounts with server admin rights may; give them in the dashboard's Users window, or create an account with them there. Admins can then give the rights to others remotely. The Uniform Chat terminal client has these in its Server menu; see its guide. The server answers at the addresses of Synapse's admin API, with the same requests and answers, so tools made for Synapse can use what is listed below; they are not tested with it, and what is not listed is missing. The dashboard over the network The server's own program opens its dashboard on a server elsewhere, with the users, rooms and reports windows. It asks for an admin's user and password, and logs that session out when it closes: uniform-chat-server manage https://matrix.example.org --user=@admin:example.org Settings and logs are reachable only on the server's machine, through its admin socket, never over the network; manage them there with sudo uniform-chat-server manage, see Run without the dashboard. The admin API is under /_synapse/admin/. A reverse proxy must forward that path too, which the example in Installing does not; add it to its location line, e.g. location ~ ^/(_matrix|_synapse/admin|\.well-known/matrix)/. Leave it out to allow administration only on the server's machine. What admins can do Area What Address Accounts List, search, show GET /_synapse/admin/v2/users, GET /_synapse/admin/v2/users/{userId} Create, or change the password, name, admin rights, lock or deactivation PUT /_synapse/admin/v2/users/{userId} Reset the password, logging out the devices POST /_synapse/admin/v1/reset_password/{userId} Admin rights GET/PUT /_synapse/admin/v1/users/{userId}/admin Deactivate: leave every room and never log in again POST /_synapse/admin/v1/deactivate/{userId} Devices, and where they last connected from GET /_matrix/client/v3/admin/whois/{userId}, also at /_synapse/admin/v1/whois/{userId} Suspend: may read, not send GET/PUT /_matrix/client/v1/admin/suspend/{userId}, also PUT /_synapse/admin/v1/suspend/{userId} Lock: every request refused until unlocked GET/PUT /_matrix/client/v1/admin/lock/{userId} Joined rooms, uploaded files GET /_synapse/admin/v1/users/{userId}/joined_rooms, …/media Registration tokens List, show, create, change, delete /_synapse/admin/v1/registration_tokens, …/new, …/{token} Reports List, show, delete /_synapse/admin/v1/event_reports, …/{id} Resolve, or open again; not in Synapse PUT /_synapse/admin/v1/event_reports/{id} with {"resolved": true} Rooms List, search, show, members GET /_synapse/admin/v1/rooms, …/{roomId}, …/{roomId}/members Block, so local users cannot join GET/PUT /_synapse/admin/v1/rooms/{roomId}/block Shut down DELETE /_synapse/admin/v1/rooms/{roomId} Files Delete an uploaded file DELETE /_synapse/admin/v1/media/{serverName}/{mediaId} Notices Send a server notice POST /_synapse/admin/v1/send_server_notice Every change is written to the server's log, so it shows which admin did what. Admins cannot suspend, lock, deactivate or take admin rights from their own account, so they cannot shut themselves out. Suspending and locking The Matrix specification defines these two ways to stop an account without deleting it: Suspended: the user can still read, leave rooms, delete their own messages and log out. The server refuses sending, joining or creating rooms, inviting, changing the profile and uploading, with the error M_USER_SUSPENDED. Use it while you look into a report. Locked: the server refuses every request of the account, and logging in, with M_USER_LOCKED, except logging out. Clients keep their session, so once you unlock the account they continue where they were. Registration tokens With Server:Registration set to Token, a new account needs a registration token. The tokens of Server:RegistrationTokens in the settings can be used any number of times and do not expire. Tokens that admins create remotely are kept in the database. Each can have a number of uses and an expiry time, and stops working when either runs out. A use is counted when a registration gets past the token step, also if the user does not finish registering. Shutting down a room Shutting a room down makes every member from this server leave and forget it, takes it out of the public room directory and deletes its addresses on this server. Blocking it also keeps this server's users from joining or being invited again. Members from other servers stay in the room, and its events stay in the database. Server notices A server notice is a message from the server to one of its users, e.g. about maintenance or changed terms. The first notice to a user creates a room named "Server notices" for them, tagged so that clients can show it apart, and only the server writes there. Later notices go to the same room while the user is in it. The notices are sent by the account @notices: followed by your server name, which the server creates without a password on the first notice. To use another name, set Server:ServerNoticesLocalpart.

articles/service.html.title: Run without the dashboard | Uniform Chat Server
articles/service.html.summary: Run without the dashboard Without a terminal, for example as a service, the server runs without the dashboard and also writes its log to standard output: ./uniform-chat-server --Host:Ui=None Host:Ui chooses the mode: Value Mode Auto (default) The dashboard when input and output are a terminal; none when either is redirected, as under systemd or with > server.log Dashboard Dashboard for monitoring server status and for perusing logs. None No dashboard. Stop the server with Ctrl+C, or with SIGTERM from a service manager. It stops within a few seconds: clients waiting for new messages get their answer at once, and the database is written out before the program ends. The log shows Stopping… and Stopped. As a user service To run the server as your own user, put the program in a folder of its own, e.g. ~/uniform-chat-server, then run it from a user unit. Its settings are in ~/.config/uniform-chat-server and its data in ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-server. Unpack the downloaded release there: mkdir -p ~/uniform-chat-server tar -xzf uniform-chat-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz -C ~/uniform-chat-server --strip-components=1 Or, from the source, publish it there: dotnet publish src/Uniform.Chat.Server -c Release -o ~/uniform-chat-server Then write the unit file: # ~/.config/systemd/user/uniform-chat-server.service [Unit] Description=Uniform Chat homeserver [Service] ExecStart=%h/uniform-chat-server/uniform-chat-server Restart=on-failure [Install] WantedBy=default.target systemctl --user enable --now uniform-chat-server journalctl --user -u uniform-chat-server -f systemd connects the server's input to /dev/null and its output to the journal, so Auto runs without the dashboard there and the log goes to the journal. A user service stops when you log out, unless lingering is on: sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER. From the apt package The uniform-chat-server package, see Installing, sets up the system service for you: What Where Program /opt/uniform-chat/server/uniform-chat-server, also as the command uniform-chat-server Service uniform-chat-server, run by the system user uniform-chat, which the package creates Settings /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json Data: database, signing key and files /var/lib/uniform-chat-server Logs: one file per start, the newest 20 kept; also in the journal, journalctl -u uniform-chat-server /var/log/uniform-chat-server The service is off after installing, as the server needs its name and address first. Write the settings, readable only by the service, as they may hold secrets, then start it and have it start at boot: sudo nano /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json sudo chown uniform-chat:uniform-chat /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json sudo chmod 600 /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json sudo systemctl enable --now uniform-chat-server Step 3 below has a short example of the settings, and Installing a complete one. The service may listen on ports below 1024, such as 443. It cannot see the home folders, so keep certificates elsewhere; the note at the end of this page tells how to give it certbot's certificates. Control it and read its log as in the table below. sudo apt upgrade restarts a running service with the new version. To change the service, e.g. to add environment variables, use sudo systemctl edit uniform-chat-server, which keeps your changes over updates. sudo apt remove uniform-chat-server stops and removes the service and the program, but keeps the settings, the data and the user. To manage the running service, open the dashboard on it; the service keeps serving meanwhile: sudo uniform-chat-server manage The manager connects through the service's admin socket, /run/uniform-chat-server/admin.sock, which only root and the uniform-chat group may open, and needs no account. It has the users, rooms and reports windows, the service's logs, and its settings. The settings work as in the dashboard, through the service itself: Apply changes the running service at once, and Save has the service write its settings file. Options marked ↻ take effect when the service starts again: sudo systemctl restart uniform-chat-server. Secrets, such as registration tokens, show as hidden and are changed only in the file. Ctrl+Q closes the manager, not the server. See Remote administration to manage a server on another machine. The dashboard of the server itself still runs when the service is stopped. Only one server runs on a data folder at a time: while the service still runs or is stopping, it exits at once with Another server (pid N) is using /var/lib/uniform-chat-server; stop it first. sudo systemctl stop uniform-chat-server sudo -u uniform-chat XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/etc XDG_DATA_HOME=/var/lib uniform-chat-server --Host:Ui=Dashboard sudo systemctl start uniform-chat-server If you set up the service by hand before, with the steps below, remove your unit file /etc/systemd/system/uniform-chat-server.service, which would otherwise be used in place of the package's, and give the settings to the new user; the service hands the data folder over itself at its next start: sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/uniform-chat-server.service sudo chown -R uniform-chat:uniform-chat /etc/uniform-chat-server sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart uniform-chat-server As a system service (Ubuntu) Without the package, set the service up by hand. On a server, run it as a system service named uniform-chat-server: it starts at boot, runs as a user of its own, and is controlled with sudo systemctl. The steps below put the program in /opt/uniform-chat-server, the settings in /etc/uniform-chat-server, and the data in /var/lib/uniform-chat-server. Create a system user for the server, with no login: sudo useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/uniform-chat-server --shell /usr/sbin/nologin uniform-chat-server Unpack the downloaded release in /opt/uniform-chat-server; or, from the source, publish it there: sudo mkdir -p /opt/uniform-chat-server sudo tar -xzf uniform-chat-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt/uniform-chat-server --strip-components=1 sudo dotnet publish src/Uniform.Chat.Server -c Release -o /opt/uniform-chat-server Write the settings to /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json, readable only by the server, as it may hold secrets such as the TURN secret. For example, behind nginx on the same machine: sudo mkdir -p /etc/uniform-chat-server sudo nano /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json sudo chown -R uniform-chat-server:uniform-chat-server /etc/uniform-chat-server sudo chmod 600 /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json { "Urls": "http://127.0.0.1:8008", "Server": { "ServerName": "example.org", "PublicBaseUrl": "https://example.org", "TrustedProxies": "127.0.0.1", "Registration": "Token", "RegistrationTokens": "a-long-random-token" } } Installing has a complete example with federation and calls, and the nginx site in front; Settings lists every option. Write the unit file /etc/systemd/system/uniform-chat-server.service: [Unit] Description=Uniform Chat homeserver After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=uniform-chat-server Group=uniform-chat-server ExecStart=/opt/uniform-chat-server/uniform-chat-server --Host:Ui=None WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/uniform-chat-server # Settings from /etc/uniform-chat-server, data in /var/lib/uniform-chat-server Environment=XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/etc Environment=XDG_DATA_HOME=/var/lib StateDirectory=uniform-chat-server StateDirectoryMode=0700 Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 # Stop gracefully: SIGTERM, then wait for the database to close TimeoutStopSec=30 # Hardening: no new privileges, read-only system, private /tmp NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true PrivateTmp=true ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/uniform-chat-server /etc/uniform-chat-server [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target The server adds its own name to XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_DATA_HOME, which gives the two folders above. /etc/uniform-chat-server is writable so that the settings window, if you ever run the dashboard as this user, can save there; take it out of ReadWritePaths to keep the settings read-only. Start it, and have it start at boot: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now uniform-chat-server Then control it with systemctl, and read its log from the journal: Command Does sudo systemctl status uniform-chat-server Show whether it runs, and the latest log lines sudo systemctl stop uniform-chat-server Stop it sudo systemctl start uniform-chat-server Start it sudo systemctl restart uniform-chat-server Restart it, e.g. after changing the settings sudo systemctl disable uniform-chat-server Not start it at boot any more journalctl -u uniform-chat-server -f Follow the log journalctl -u uniform-chat-server --since today Today's log The server also keeps its own log files in /var/lib/uniform-chat-server/logs, with its database and signing key; see Files. To update the server, see Updating. Note To serve HTTPS itself, without a proxy, the server needs to read the certificate and to listen on port 443: Ports below 1024 need AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in the [Service] section, which the package's service has; or listen on 8448 instead. certbot keeps its files readable only by root. Copy them where the server can read them in a deploy hook, e.g. /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/uniform-chat-server.sh; with the package, the user is uniform-chat: #!/bin/sh install -o uniform-chat-server -g uniform-chat-server -m 600 "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/fullchain.pem" "$RENEWED_LINEAGE/privkey.pem" /etc/uniform-chat-server/tls/ and point Tls:CertificatePath and Tls:KeyPath at /etc/uniform-chat-server/tls/. The server picks up renewed files without a restart.

articles/settings.html.title: Settings | Uniform Chat Server
articles/settings.html.summary: Settings Settings come from these places; later ones override earlier ones: appsettings.json next to the program ~/.config/uniform-chat-server/settings.json, written by the settings window Environment variables, with __ between parts: Server__Registration=Open The command line: --Server:Registration=Open Changes applied in the settings window, until the server stops Option Default Meaning Urls http://localhost:8008 Addresses to listen on, separated by ;. ↻ Server:ServerName localhost The name in user IDs and room aliases, such as example.org in @alice:example.org. Choose it before creating accounts: changing it later leaves every existing account and room behind. ↻ Server:PublicBaseUrl not set The address clients should use, such as https://matrix.example.org. When set, the server announces it at /.well-known/matrix/client. Server:Registration Disabled Who can create accounts: Disabled, Open (anyone), or Token (anyone with a registration token). Server:TrustedProxies not set Addresses of reverse proxies, such as nginx, whose X-Forwarded-For header gives the client's address, separated by commas. Set it when the server runs behind a proxy, so rate limits count each client instead of the proxy. Other senders' headers are ignored. ↻ Server:RegistrationTokens not set Tokens for Token registration, separated by commas; admins can also create tokens with limited uses remotely. Server:TermsUrl not set Address of terms of service that new users accept when registering. Server:PrivacyPolicyUrl not set Address of a privacy policy that new users accept when registering. Server:PoliciesVersion 1.0 Version of the terms and privacy policy; raise it when they change. Server:ServerNoticesLocalpart notices Name of the account that sends server notices, created without a password on the first notice. Media:MaxUploadSize 52428800 Largest file users can upload, in bytes (50 MiB). Media:MaxThumbnailSourcePixels 40000000 Largest image, in pixels, that thumbnails are made from; larger images get none. Media:AllowUnauthenticatedDownloads false Also serve files at the old /_matrix/media/v3 download addresses, which need no login, for older clients. Anyone with a link can then fetch a file, so leave it off unless a client needs it. Media:PendingUploadLifetime 1.00:00:00 How long a client may take to upload a file it reserved an address for first. Media:MaxPendingUploads 10 How many reserved addresses a user may have waiting for their files. Push:AllowPrivateGateways false Send push notifications also to gateways at private and local network addresses, such as a push gateway on this machine. Off, so accounts cannot make the server reach machines inside your network. Push:GatewayTimeout 00:00:10 How long to wait for a push gateway to answer. UrlPreviews:Enabled false Make previews of linked pages (title, description and image) for clients that ask. Off by default: fetching tells the linked site that someone on this server posted the link, and in encrypted rooms it shows the server what was linked. UrlPreviews:AllowPrivateAddresses false Also preview pages at private and local network addresses. Off, so accounts cannot make the server reach machines inside your network. UrlPreviews:MaxSize 2097152 Most bytes read of a page or its image (2 MiB). UrlPreviews:Timeout 00:00:10 How long to wait for a page. UrlPreviews:CacheDuration 01:00:00 How long a preview is reused for the same address. RateLimits:Enabled true Limit how fast clients may write and log in. Clients that go over get an error telling them how long to wait; well-behaved clients wait and retry. ↻ RateLimits:WriteBurst 50 Writes per login allowed at once: messages, state changes, invites, new rooms and uploads. ↻ RateLimits:WritesPerSecond 10 Writes per login allowed each second after the burst. ↻ RateLimits:LoginBurst 20 Logins and registrations from one address allowed at once. Behind a reverse proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so these limits are shared by everyone. ↻ RateLimits:LoginsPerMinute 10 Logins and registrations from one address allowed each minute after the burst. ↻ Federation:Enabled false Talk to other Matrix servers: profiles, joining their rooms by ID or alias, invites both ways, messages, files and images, end-to-end encryption, typing, read receipts and presence. Still being built: received events are checked against the room's current state only, and state differences between servers are not resolved yet. Needs HTTPS with a real certificate. Federation:AllowPrivateAddresses false Also reach servers at private and local network addresses. Off, so remote server names cannot make the server reach machines inside your network. Federation:TrustedKeyServers not set Key servers to ask for other servers' signing keys when those servers cannot be reached, separated by commas, such as matrix.org. Asking tells the key server which servers this one talks to, so none are asked by default. With one set, joining a large room is much faster, as the keys of all its servers come in a few requests. Federation:RequestTimeout 00:00:30 How long to wait for another server to answer. Federation:JoinTimeout 00:03:00 How long to wait for another server to answer a join, which sends the whole state of the room. Federation:KeyRequestTimeout 00:00:10 How long to wait for a server's signing keys, from it or a key server. Federation:KeyValidity 1.00:00:00 How long other servers may keep this server's signing key before asking again. Federation:WellKnownServer not set Where other servers should connect, served as /.well-known/matrix/server, such as example.org:443 when a reverse proxy on port 443 forwards to this server. Needed when the server name has no port and the server is not on port 8448. Calls:LiveKitServiceUrl not set Address of the MatrixRTC authorization service (lk-jwt-service) in front of a LiveKit server, for calls in Element X and other MatrixRTC clients. Announced to clients through rtc/transports and /.well-known/matrix/client. With LiveKit:Enabled, the built-in service at /livekit/jwt of Server:PublicBaseUrl when not set. Calls:TurnUris not set TURN server addresses for older 1:1 calls, separated by commas, such as turn:turn.example.org:3478?transport=udp. Calls:TurnSharedSecret not set Shared secret of the TURN server, such as coturn's static-auth-secret. Keep it out of command lines; set it in the settings file or as the environment variable Calls__TurnSharedSecret. Calls:TurnUserLifetime 1.00:00:00 How long TURN credentials hold. Calls:MaxEventDelay 1.00:00:00 Longest delay of a delayed event, which calls use to end the membership of a client that disappears. Delayed events are kept in the database, so a restart does not lose them; those due while the server was down are sent when it starts. Calls:OpenIdTokenLifetime 01:00:00 How long an OpenID token holds; call services use these tokens to check who a user is. LiveKit:Enabled false Serve the built-in MatrixRTC authorization service at /livekit/jwt, which gives Element X and other MatrixRTC clients tokens of your LiveKit server. See Video calls in Element X. LiveKit:Url not set Address of the LiveKit server that clients join, such as wss://livekit.example.org. LiveKit:ApiKey not set API key of the LiveKit server, one of the keys in its configuration. LiveKit:ApiSecret not set Secret of that API key. Keep it out of command lines; set it in the settings file or as the environment variable LiveKit__ApiSecret. LiveKit:FullAccessHomeservers not set Homeservers whose users may start calls and send audio and video, separated by commas, or * for all; users of other servers can only watch and listen in calls that are already going. This server's name when not set. LiveKit:TokenLifetime 01:00:00 How long a LiveKit token can be used to join; a call that has started goes on. LiveKit:CanUpdateOwnMetadata false Let participants change their own name and metadata in LiveKit. Turn:Enabled false Run the built-in STUN and TURN server, which relays calls between users whose networks would block them; calls then use it unless Calls:TurnUris names another. See Calls through firewalls. ↻ Turn:Realm not set Realm of the TURN credentials; the server name when not set. ↻ Turn:ListenAddress 0.0.0.0 Address the TURN server listens on. ↻ Turn:Port 3478 Port of STUN and TURN over UDP and TCP. ↻ Turn:Tcp true Also listen over TCP on that port, for networks that block UDP. ↻ Turn:TlsPort not set Port of TURN over TLS, such as 5349; none when not set. ↻ Turn:CertificatePath not set Certificate file of TURN over TLS; that of Tls:CertificatePath when not set. ↻ Turn:KeyPath not set Private key of that certificate; that of Tls:KeyPath when not set. ↻ Turn:ExternalAddress not set Public IPv4 address that relayed data is sent to, the router's public address when the server is behind NAT: a fixed address, a host name that is resolved again at every check, or stun:host:port to ask that STUN server. The host of Server:PublicBaseUrl, or else the server name, when not set. A changed address, e.g. after the router's DHCP lease, goes to new relays. ↻ Turn:AddressCheckInterval 00:01:00 How often the TURN server checks its local and public addresses for changes, besides when the system reports one. ↻ Turn:RelayAddress not set Address the relay ports bind; the listen address when not set. ↻ Turn:MinRelayPort 49152 First UDP port of relayed addresses. ↻ Turn:MaxRelayPort 65535 Last UDP port of relayed addresses; behind NAT, forward the whole range. ↻ Turn:MaxAllocations 1000 Most relays at once; a call uses one or two. ↻ Turn:MaxAllocationsPerUser 10 Most relays at once per user. ↻ Turn:AllowedPeers not set Private addresses relayed to anyway, separated by commas, such as 192.168.1.0/24; private, loopback and link-local addresses are refused otherwise, so outsiders cannot reach your network through the server. ↻ Turn:SharedSecrets not set Further shared secrets of time-limited credentials, for other services than this homeserver. ↻ Turn:Users not set Fixed users as name:password, separated by commas. Keep them out of command lines. ↻ Tls:CertificatePath not set Certificate file for https:// addresses in Urls, with its intermediate certificates, such as certbot's fullchain.pem. A path may start with ~/ for the home folder, also where the shell leaves it alone, as in --Tls:CertificatePath=~/tls/fullchain.pem. A renewed file is picked up within a minute, without a restart. ↻ Tls:KeyPath not set Private key of the certificate, such as certbot's privkey.pem. Keep it readable only by the account that runs the server. ↻ Storage:DataDirectory ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-server Folder for the database, signing key, media and logs. ↻ Storage:DatabaseFileName server.db Database file inside the data folder. ↻ Storage:MediaDirectoryName media Folder inside the data folder for uploaded files. ↻ Storage:LogDirectoryName logs Folder inside the data folder with one log file per session. ↻ Storage:LogDirectory none Folder for the session logs anywhere, in place of the one inside the data folder; the apt package's service uses /var/log/uniform-chat-server. ↻ Storage:LogFilesKept 20 How many session logs to keep. ↻ Host:Ui Auto Auto, Dashboard or None, see Run without the dashboard. ↻ Host:AdminSocket none A local socket for uniform-chat-server manage --socket=PATH, e.g. /run/uniform-chat-server/admin.sock, which the service uses. Whoever may open it manages the server as an admin, without an account; the server lets only its own user and group open it. ↻ Logging:LogLevel:Default Information Lowest level written to the log: Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical or None. ↻ marks options that take effect after a restart. Warning Without Tls:* the server speaks plain HTTP. Keep it on localhost, or give it a certificate, or put a reverse proxy such as Caddy or nginx in front of it, before letting other computers connect. Listening on all interfaces (--Urls=http://0.0.0.0:8008) without HTTPS sends passwords unencrypted. To serve HTTPS itself, point the server at a certificate, for example certbot's files, and use https:// addresses: ./uniform-chat-server --Urls="https://0.0.0.0:8448" \ --Tls:CertificatePath=/path/to/fullchain.pem --Tls:KeyPath=/path/to/privkey.pem

articles/troubleshooting.html.title: Troubleshooting | Uniform Chat Server
articles/troubleshooting.html.summary: Troubleshooting Message Meaning Cannot listen on http://localhost:8008: the address is already in use Another program, perhaps another copy of the server, uses the port. Stop it, or choose another port with --Urls=http://localhost:8009. M_FORBIDDEN: Registration is disabled. Set Server:Registration to Open or Token. M_USER_IN_USE The user name is taken; choose another. ... is not an ed25519 signing key. signing.key was changed or damaged. Restore it from a backup. Running without dashboard: input is redirected; --Host:Ui=Dashboard forces it The server was started without a terminal, for example from an IDE's run button or with redirected input or output. Run it from a terminal, or use --Host:Ui=Dashboard to force the dashboard.

articles/turn.html.title: Calls through firewalls | Uniform Chat Server
articles/turn.html.summary: Calls through firewalls Voice calls go straight from one phone or computer to the other when the networks allow it. Many don't: mobile networks, office firewalls and some home routers block such direct traffic, and then the call connects but nobody hears anything. A TURN server fixes this by relaying the call. The server has one built in, which your users' calls use as soon as it is on. Element X and other apps that call through Element Call use a LiveKit server instead, see Video calls in Element X. Turning it on The server must be reachable from the internet on these ports: Port Protocol Use 3478 UDP and TCP STUN and TURN, Turn:Port 49152–65535 UDP Relayed calls, Turn:MinRelayPort to Turn:MaxRelayPort 5349, if set TCP TURN over TLS, Turn:TlsPort Behind a home router, forward these ports to the server's computer. A smaller relay range is easier to forward and is enough for a small server; each call uses one or two ports: ./uniform-chat-server --Turn:Enabled=true --Turn:MinRelayPort=50000 --Turn:MaxRelayPort=50099 The server then hands out credentials for its own TURN server to every call, with addresses made from the host name of Server:PublicBaseUrl. It needs to know the public address that relayed calls are sent to, Turn:ExternalAddress. When not set, it is looked up from that host name, which is right when the name points at your router. Set it when the name points elsewhere, e.g. at a proxy on another machine: ./uniform-chat-server --Turn:Enabled=true --Turn:ExternalAddress=203.0.113.5 The log tells where it listens: TURN server listening on udp 0.0.0.0:3478, tcp 0.0.0.0:3478, relaying from 203.0.113.5 ports 50000-50099 When a setting is wrong, the log says so and the homeserver runs on without the TURN server. Changing addresses Home connections often get a new public address now and then, e.g. when the router renews its DHCP lease or restarts. The server checks every minute, and whenever the computer's own addresses change. A host name in Turn:ExternalAddress, as of a dynamic DNS service, is resolved again then, and relays made after a change get the new address. Calls going on at the change break anyway, as the old address no longer reaches your router; the apps connect them again. A dynamic DNS name can lag behind a change. To ask a STUN server instead, which sees the new address at once, set Turn:ExternalAddress=stun:stun.example.org:3478, naming a STUN server you trust. The server also follows its own addresses: listening on 0.0.0.0, the default, it starts listening on a new address of the computer and stops on one that is gone. Over TLS Some networks only let web traffic through. TURN over TLS gets through more of them, especially on port 443 when nothing else uses that port on the address: ./uniform-chat-server --Turn:Enabled=true --Turn:TlsPort=5349 It uses the certificate of Tls:CertificatePath and Tls:KeyPath, or of Turn:CertificatePath and Turn:KeyPath. A renewed certificate is used without a restart. Safety Only your users can use the relay: each call gets credentials that expire after Calls:TurnUserLifetime. The server refuses to relay to private, loopback and link-local addresses, so nobody can reach your local network through it, and limits how many relays a user and the whole server may have. Turn:AllowedPeers lets calls reach chosen private addresses anyway, e.g. when the users of a local network call each other through it. Another TURN server To use another TURN server, such as coturn or uniform-stun-server, the standalone TURN server of this project, leave Turn:Enabled off and set Calls:TurnUris and Calls:TurnSharedSecret. The secret must be the same on both servers: static-auth-secret of coturn, Turn:SharedSecrets of uniform-stun-server.

articles/updating.html.title: Updating | Uniform Chat Server
articles/updating.html.summary: Updating The server updates its database to the new version's layout when it starts. Back up the data folder before updating: it holds the database and the signing key, which other servers know your server by. From the apt package Back up the data, then update with the rest of the system; a running service restarts with the new version: sudo tar -czf ~/uniform-chat-server-backup.tar.gz -C /var/lib uniform-chat-server sudo apt update sudo apt upgrade To go back to an earlier version, give it, e.g. sudo apt install uniform-chat-server=0.2.0; apt list -a uniform-chat-server lists them. An earlier version may not work with a database that a later one updated, so restore the backup with it. As a system service Stop the server, back up its data, unpack the new release over the program, and start it: sudo systemctl stop uniform-chat-server sudo tar -czf ~/uniform-chat-server-backup.tar.gz -C /var/lib uniform-chat-server sudo tar -xzf uniform-chat-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt/uniform-chat-server --strip-components=1 sudo systemctl start uniform-chat-server Run by hand or as a user service Stop the server, copy ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-server somewhere safe, unpack the new release over the program's folder, and start the server again. From a version before the name Uniform Chat Before Uniform Chat, the program was Uniform.Matrix.Server.Host and its folders were named uniform-matrix-server-host. The new version does not look in the old folders: started as it is, it would begin with an empty database and a new signing key. Move the folders first. Run by hand or as a user service Stop the server, then rename its settings and data folders: mv ~/.config/uniform-matrix-server-host ~/.config/uniform-chat-server mv ~/.local/share/uniform-matrix-server-host ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-server Unpack the new release, and start uniform-chat-server where you started Uniform.Matrix.Server.Host, e.g. in the ExecStart of a user unit. Settings that name files in the old folders, such as Tls:CertificatePath, need the new folder too. As a system service A system service set up with the earlier guide is named uniform-matrix, runs as the user uniform-matrix, and keeps its program in /opt/uniform-matrix, its settings in /etc/uniform-matrix/uniform-matrix-server-host and its data in /var/lib/uniform-matrix/uniform-matrix-server-host. To move it to the names of Run without the dashboard: Stop and disable the old service, and back up its data: sudo systemctl disable --now uniform-matrix sudo tar -czf ~/uniform-matrix-backup.tar.gz -C /var/lib uniform-matrix -C /etc uniform-matrix Rename the user and its group, which keeps the owner of the files: sudo usermod -l uniform-chat-server -d /var/lib/uniform-chat-server uniform-matrix sudo groupmod -n uniform-chat-server uniform-matrix Move the settings and the data; TLS files too, if the server reads them itself: sudo mv /etc/uniform-matrix/uniform-matrix-server-host /etc/uniform-chat-server sudo mv /var/lib/uniform-matrix/uniform-matrix-server-host /var/lib/uniform-chat-server sudo mv /etc/uniform-matrix/tls /etc/uniform-chat-server/tls Then change paths in /etc/uniform-chat-server/settings.json that point into the old folders, such as Tls:CertificatePath and Tls:KeyPath, and the certbot deploy hook, if there is one. Unpack the new release in /opt/uniform-chat-server: sudo mkdir -p /opt/uniform-chat-server sudo tar -xzf uniform-chat-server-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz -C /opt/uniform-chat-server --strip-components=1 Replace the unit file: remove /etc/systemd/system/uniform-matrix.service, write /etc/systemd/system/uniform-chat-server.service as in Run without the dashboard, and start it: sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/uniform-matrix.service sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now uniform-chat-server sudo systemctl status uniform-chat-server Once it runs with your accounts and rooms, remove what is left of the old layout: sudo rm -r /opt/uniform-matrix /etc/uniform-matrix /var/lib/uniform-matrix The nginx site needs no change, as long as the server listens at the same address.

articles/usermanagement.html.title: User Management | Uniform Chat Server
articles/usermanagement.html.summary: User Management The server starts with registration disabled, so nobody can create an account by themselves. The simplest way to add people is the dashboard: Server → Users → New (see Users window). To let people register in their own account: Start the server with registration open, or with tokens: ./uniform-chat-server --Server:Registration=Open ./uniform-chat-server --Server:Registration=Token --Server:RegistrationTokens=let-me-in Or change Server:Registration in the settings window and Apply, as above. Register in a client that lets you type the homeserver address, such as the Uniform Chat apps or Element Desktop: choose "Create account", give the homeserver http://localhost:8008, and with Token the token. Close registration again when you are done. To have new users accept your terms of service or privacy policy, set Server:TermsUrl and Server:PrivacyPolicyUrl to the addresses of the documents. Registering then shows them with their links, and the account is created only after the user accepts them. When you change the documents, raise Server:PoliciesVersion. Deleting accounts Users can delete their own account from their client, confirming with their password; in the Uniform Chat apps, see their guides. The account is deactivated: the user leaves every room, their display name and avatar are cleared, every device is logged out, and the password no longer works. The user ID stays taken, so nobody can register it again and pose as them. Messages they sent stay in the rooms. The admin can deactivate and reactivate accounts in the dashboard's Users window. From a client Accounts with server admin rights can also manage accounts, registration tokens, reports and rooms from a client, e.g. the Server menu of the Uniform Chat terminal client. They can suspend or lock accounts, and send server notices. See Remote administration. Registration also works from the command line: curl -X POST http://localhost:8008/_matrix/client/v3/register \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"username":"alice","password":"choose-a-password","auth":{"type":"m.login.dummy"}}' For Token registration, use "auth":{"type":"m.login.registration_token","token":"let-me-in"}. The new user is @alice:localhost, or @alice: followed by the configured server name. Their display name starts out as their user name. Configure from dashboard When the server runs as a system service from the apt package, open the dashboard on the running service in a terminal; the service keeps serving meanwhile: sudo uniform-chat-server manage

index.html.title: Server | Uniform Chat Server
index.html.summary: Uniform Chat Server A homeserver for Matrix, the open chat protocol. It runs with a dashboard in the terminal, or without one as a service. Accounts, rooms, messages, sync, profiles, typing, receipts, the room directory, files and end-to-end encryption work; federation with other servers is being built and is off by default. Note The server is in early development. Keep its registration closed, and do not rely on it for important conversations yet. Installing: what the server does and how to install it. Run with the dashboard: the terminal dashboard and its windows. Run without the dashboard: as a background or systemd service. Settings: every setting and where settings come from. User Management: creating accounts and registration. Connecting clients: the address clients use. Files: where the database, keys, media and logs are. Updating: new versions, and moving a server from the names before Uniform Chat. Troubleshooting: common problems. For apps to chat with, see the guides of the app for Windows, Linux and Android and the terminal client.
